# About the Data

**The dataset in this project is synthetic. It was generated by
`scripts/generate_data.py` and does not describe any real product, any
real company, or any real users.**

Please read every number in this repository with that in mind. Nothing
here is evidence about real-world product behaviour, real customer
retention, or real business impact.

## Why synthetic data

The project had a fixed ten-hour budget. Using generated data kept that
time on the analysis — metric definitions, SQL, and the dashboard —
rather than on sourcing and cleaning a real dataset.

Purely random data would have been useless, because every metric would
land on the same value in every segment and there would be nothing to
find. So the generator deliberately builds in behavioural differences
between segments and a decline over time, and the SQL then measures
them. The patterns the analysis reports were designed into the data.

## What this means for the findings

The findings in this project demonstrate **method**, not discovery. The
value on show is the reasoning: how the metrics were defined, how the
denominators were chosen, how a measurement error was caught and
corrected, and how the results were turned into questions a product team
could act on.

The same queries pointed at a real event table would produce real
findings. The numbers here would not.

## Reproducibility

The generator uses a fixed random seed, so the dataset is exactly
reproducible:

```bash
python3 scripts/generate_data.py   # writes data/raw/*.csv
./scripts/load_data.sh             # rebuilds the schema and loads PostgreSQL
psql -d insightflow -f sql/00_validate.sql
./scripts/export_metrics.sh        # writes data/tableau/*.csv
```

`data/raw/` is not committed because it is regenerable from the seed.
The aggregated CSVs in `data/tableau/` are committed, since the Tableau
workbook reads them.

## Correlation and causation

Several results in this project are associations between two things
measured on the same users, not causal relationships. The clearest
example is early core-feature adoption and conversion: users who reach
the core feature in their first week also subscribe more often, but they
were not randomly assigned to do so, and the same underlying interest
plausibly explains both.

Statements of the form "X is associated with Y, and is worth
investigating" are supported by this analysis. Statements of the form
"X causes Y" or "doing more of X will improve Y" are not. Establishing
that would require an experiment.
